analysis.one_liner: Sets federal standards and anti-fraud rules for long-term care insurance sold to seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 53 cosponsors from both parties and three subcommittee hearings, but the House committee never voted on it before Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every long-term care insurance policy sold in the U.S. to meet federal or state-approved standards. Policies would have to be guaranteed renewable, include inflation protection, cap premium increases, use plain standard language, and give buyers 30 days to return the policy for a refund. It would also ban high-pressure sales tactics, prohibit selling policies to people on Medicaid who don't need them, cap agent commissions, and require states to run a regulatory program — with states that refuse risking some Medicaid funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Older Americans shopping for long-term care insurance, a product that in the early 1990s was frequently sold with confusing terms, misleading claims, and policies that covered far less than buyers believed. The bill would give them standardized disclosures, guaranteed renewability, appeals rights when claims or home care are denied, protection against discrimination based on Alzheimer's disease, and refunds if they change their mind within 30 days.

how_it_helps.text: Policies would have to be guaranteed renewable — insurers could not cancel them for any reason other than nonpayment of premiums or material misrepresentation [S3].

Every policy must include inflation protection of at least 5% a year and state a specific cap on annual premium increases, so buyers know the coverage will not shrink and premiums cannot jump without limit [S3].
Buyers get a 30-day 'free look' to return the policy for a full refund, an outline of coverage in uniform plain language, and the right to appeal a denial of home care benefits [S3].

The bill bans high-pressure sales tactics, misleading comparisons between policies ('twisting'), and deceptive ads that hide that the caller is an insurance salesman, and it makes selling a policy to a Medicaid beneficiary illegal [S3].

People with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias could not be treated differently in benefits than people with other conditions, and preexisting-condition exclusions would be limited to six months [S3].

States must establish regulatory programs enforcing these standards with consumer access to complaint records and public review of premium increases; states that fail could lose some federal Medicaid funds for nursing facility services [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Long-term care insurers and their agents. Insurers would bear compliance costs, civil fines of up to $25,000 per violation (and criminal penalties for sales-practice violations), disclosure and reporting requirements, and a cap on first-year agent commissions. Some low-value policies that depended on aggressive marketing to be profitable would likely have been pulled from the market.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a state system replace the federal one: if a state establishes a qualifying regulatory program, its own insurance commissioner approves policies, so the strength of protection would vary by state [S3].

The standards-writing process leans on the National Association of Insurance Commissioners — a private body of state regulators — with HHS stepping in only if the NAIC misses a 12-month deadline, adding a layer of industry-familiar negotiation through a consultation group that includes issuers [S3].

Stricter product requirements — mandatory inflation protection, nonforfeiture benefits, capped commissions — would likely raise premiums for some buyers, and insurers argued compliance costs could push marginal products off the market, shrinking choices [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address real, well-documented harm: long-term care policies in this era were notorious for opaque terms, premium shocks, and denials of exactly the home care benefits buyers thought they had. The main honest cost is on the supply side — higher compliance costs and commission caps, which could mean higher premiums or fewer cheap, low-benefit products. For a product bought by people at their most vulnerable, uniform disclosure, guaranteed renewability, and a 30-day refund right are low-tech, high-value protections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in House subcommittees — it got three hearings over a year and a half, but the Energy and Commerce Committee never voted to send it to the House floor before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Ron Wyden introduced the bill on April 17, 1991, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S1] [S5].
It was split between two subcommittees — Health and the Environment, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness — in May 1991 [S5].
Three subcommittee hearings were held: October 1991, May 1992, and July 1992, but the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a House vote [S5].

The bill had 53 cosponsors across party lines (44 Democrats, 8 Republicans, 1 Independent), including Republicans such as Claudine Schneider and leading figures like Ed Markey and Charles Rangel as original cosponsors [S4] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Long-term care insurers and sales agents, who could keep selling policies under the loose, uneven state rules of the time without federal standards, commission caps, or federal penalties — while seniors kept bearing the risk of confusing or inadequate coverage.

for.name: Rep. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Long-Term Care Insurance Consumer Protection Act of 1991 and led it through the House.

for.name: 53 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill across party lines, including original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce subcommittees
for.role: Subcommittees on Health and the Environment, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness
for.what_they_did: Held three hearings on the bill between October 1991 and July 1992.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; despite hearings, no markup or vote was ever scheduled, keeping it off the House floor.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not advance the bill; a bill that never leaves committee cannot reach the floor without leadership action, and none came.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 53 cosponsors split 44 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 Independent, with Republicans among the original cosponsors — so the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have forced every policy to meet federal standards — guaranteed renewability, inflation protection, premium-increase limits, plain-language disclosure — and imposed fines up to $25,000 per violation, plus criminal penalties for abusive sales practices. Insurers' interest in keeping loosely regulated, aggressively marketed products ran directly against protections for the seniors buying them.

industries.industry: Insurance agents selling long-term care policies
industries.note: The bill caps first-year commissions at 200% of renewal-year compensation, counts bonuses, prizes, and gifts as compensation, bans high-pressure tactics and completing applicants' medical histories, and requires reporting of lapse and denial rates by agent. Much of the marketing that made the product lucrative for agents is what the bill targeted.

States must build regulatory programs enforcing the standards or risk losing some federal Medicaid nursing-facility funding, but a functioning program reduces the flow of seniors who bought useless coverage and ended up on Medicaid anyway. The bill also bans selling new policies to current Medicaid beneficiaries.
